## Notes

Attribution run for the accepted write-lifecycle tail (issue #430). Measured against the same stack the committed
reference was recorded on (`aanbrn/axon-showcase-*:0.2.0-SNAPSHOT`, app pods created 2026-10-08T02:24Z), rate-matched to
its operating point (`CALIBRATE_MAX_RATE=200`, 127 vs 127 workload units/s, ~239 rps, 144,258 requests). The plateau ran
07:44:56–07:54:56Z (the baseline profile's own injection span); the host's load average at run start was 12.0 / 13.2 /
10.3 across 10 cores. The reference is restored as recorded.

**The tail did not compound — the write-lifecycle p99 fell back.** Every request whose p99 the 2026-10-08 refresh
accepted improved or held: `PollShowcase` 56 → 22 ms, `StartShowcase` 45 → 24, `ScheduleShowcase` 29 → 22,
`RemoveShowcase` 30 → 29. The other three moved by a millisecond or three: `FetchShowcase` 22 → 25, `FinishShowcase` 27
→ 28, and the list read 14 → 11. The aggregate plateau p99 is 15 ms against that run's 20. Across the four recorded runs
the write-lifecycle p99 series is poll 12 / 24 / 56 / 22 and start 10 / 18 / 45 / 24 — a spread around a stable level,
not a trend, which is what the 2026-10-08 record's "tail noise" reading guessed at without per-request evidence.

**The services' own server side is about half the figure, and the excess is in the tail.** Read from the Prometheus
series over the plateau's window
(`histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, uri, method) (increase(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[…][600s])))`, and the
mean as `sum(increase(sum)) / sum(increase(count))`):

| route                    | server mean | server p99 | client mean | client p99 |
| ------------------------ | ----------- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| GET `/showcases`         | 1.2 ms      | 6.7 ms     | 2 ms        | 11 ms      |
| POST `/showcases`        | 4.8 ms      | 14.7 ms    | 7 ms        | 22 ms      |
| GET `/showcases/{id}`    | 3.4 ms      | 10.2 ms    | 3–5 ms      | 22–25 ms   |
| PUT `…/start`            | 3.7 ms      | 11.1 ms    | 5 ms        | 24 ms      |
| PUT `…/finish`           | 4.3 ms      | 13.0 ms    | 6 ms        | 28 ms      |
| DELETE `/showcases/{id}` | 3.9 ms      | 13.0 ms    | 6 ms        | 29 ms      |

The client mean exceeds the server mean by up to about 2 ms (the blended by-id row straddles its server figure), while
the client p99 is about twice the server p99, so the excess grows in the tail rather than in the work. The
command-service's own handling sits below that (`commandBus_successTimer` p99 8.0 ms, mean 1.8 ms), so the write service
is not the tail's source; per-service CPU stayed low, the busiest being the gateway at 5.3% of the node's cores
(`process_cpu_usage` is a fraction of all CPUs, so that peak is ≈0.5 core).

**What this does not establish.** The p99-scope gap lies outside the gateway's handler; the candidates are the gateway's
own transport path (`http_server_requests_seconds` is handler-scoped, so its decode, read, and flush are inside the
delta), the Gatling client's JVM, which shares this host, the local network, and the ingress this target resolves
through — none of which is measured here. Process-level stalls do exist in the environment: one command-service pod
logged a 360 ms p99 GC pause over the plateau (20 ms on its sibling, 7–8 ms elsewhere), and the plateau's own extreme
tail is a handful of requests — 12 of its ~144,000 exceeded 500 ms (5 of them POST `/showcases`, 3 `…/start`, 3
`…/finish`, 1 DELETE) against the client-side maximum of 654 ms — so the stalls and the slowest requests are of the same
order. One run cannot separate a scheduling tail from a pause tail, and that the suspected host is also the measuring
host is the limit of any measurement taken on it.

Two pairs are blended in the server-side figures: `FetchShowcase` and `PollShowcase` both GET `/showcases/{showcaseId}`,
so that row covers either request and only the client-side figures separate them, and `ScheduleShowcase` and
`SeedShowcase` both POST `/showcases`, where the seed is one request per run and so contributes negligibly.

**Consequence.** The drift check compares this client-side p99, so roughly half of what it tracks is the client and host
rather than the pipeline, and its run-to-run spread is wide (poll 12–56 ms across four runs). Whether the comparison
keeps tracking that figure, tracks a less noisy one, or requires a regression to confirm before it fails was a change to
the drift requirement's own sensitivity — settled afterwards by `make-the-p99-verdict-confirm-first` (issue #571), which
makes a p99-only excursion unconfirmed rather than a regression.
